title.narrative: Water Network Restructuring And Rehabilitation

description.narrative:
Jordan - Water Network Restructuring And Rehabilitation project: In 2007, the wastewater collection system in Zarqa Governorate was limited in reach and endangered public health. The system frequently overflowed into city streets and the surrounding environment, relied on pump stations that had insufficient capacity, and did not serve nearly 30 percent of the population. The Wastewater Network Project represented the largest investment in wastewater infrastructure improvements for Zarqa Governorate system. The objectives of the project were to (i) increase access to the wastewater network, (ii) increase the volume of wastewater collected within Zarqa Governorate for treatment and reuse, and (iii) reduce the incidents of sewage overflow.
The Wastewater Network Project was originally comprised of two activities: (i) the reinforcement of existing networks and rehabilitation of existing sewer main lines in West Zarqa, and (ii) the reinforcement of existing networks and rehabilitation of existing sewer main lines in East Zarqa.
The project extended service to households that were not connected to the sewer network by constructing over 300 kilometers of new sewers in the neighborhoods of East Zarqa and West Zarqa, both of which lacked access to the sewer network. The extension of lateral sewer lines raised wastewater service coverage rates from 72 percent to about 84 percent of the local Jordanian population, though coverage rates of the full population dropped due to the influx of Syrian and Iraqi refugees. These new customer connections also generated additional wastewater. The project provided more than 8,700 connection points to the wastewater pipes, which allowed over 54,800 people to be connected to the new wastewater system. These new customer connections generated additional wastewater which is treated at the As-Samra Wastewater Treatment Plant and reused in agriculture downstream in the Jordan Valley. The project also utilized unused budget identified during implementation of the compact to add 65 kilometers of pipes to the Princess Haya neighborhood of the Zarqa Governorate and to purchase high pressure jet cleaning vehicles for the water utility to enhance system maintenance.

description.narrative: Level Outcome of '- Miyahuna Zarqa does not calculate the specific supply time for its distribution areas. Instead, Miyahunna Zarqa issues a table for water distribution rounds. The table notifies the public of the expected timing to receive their water according to the water schedule. The latest schedule was as of April 28 and lasts through summer time. The table does not specifiy a specific hour for the supply duration, rather than provide an approximate time on when to expect the water supply. The reported supply time is said to have stayed at 36 hrs per week, however MCC cannot find accurate documentation to verify this value. Due to these unexpected documentation concerns, MCC will only be reporting the supply schedule provided once Miyahuna overtook the management of the WAJ utility in 2015. Supply schedules are provided by area, including the hours and number of people in each area. A weighted average calculation uses the hours in the supply schedule (depending on how many people are in each area, and given that smaller population areas will have lower areas of supply) to find the average hours of supply across all areas and total population. This calculation differs for summer and winter time, and MCA-J makes the assumption that winter consumption of water (which is higher) is 30% higher. MCC (upon the recommendation of Miyahuna and MCA-J staff) have decided to remove the 36 hours of supply documented in the ITT prior to Q20.<br>-This indicator reports the operation hours per week as scheduled by Miyahuna Zarqa based on the supply rotation for Zarqa.<br>- The annual calculation for % complete will be taken as an average over all four quarters in order to account for seasonal variation.

title.narrative: Kilometers of pipelines that are expanded, reinforced or rehabilitated (Ruseifa)

description.narrative: Cumulative Output of '- Data source are the PMC reports (which include all km of pipelines constructed until 2016, and are divided into TOTAL primary and secondary, as well as tertiary pipelines constructed by Ruseifa, Batrawi, and Zarqa). The C1 contract, for construction in primary and secondary pipelines only, was extended from August 2016 to September 2016 and the WNP project lead has provided an additional word document showing the pipes (primary and secondary) constructed up until September 2016 when final works were completed. Geographically, Batrawi pipes are embedded within Zarqa pipes; it is thus possible to deduce the total number of pipelines constructed (by Q20) using the word document (C1 contract) for primary and secondary pipelines, and the PMC report (as of August 2016 when tertiary pipes were completed) for tertiary pipelines. - All other quarterly totals of pipelines are calculated using the PMC report. - As a result of the way documentation and data is constructed, it is only possible to disaggregate pipelines built per area in Q20 when works were completed. Unfortunately there is no way to break out at which point in time pipelines were constructed in certain areas. - Actuals are recorded starting March of 2014 when works began.

description.narrative: Cumulative Output of '- Pending the revision of the M&E Plan in December 2016, it was agreed that Miyahuna would provide data on customer meters for non MCC DMAs for the areas of Ruseifa, Batrawi, and Zarqa. Reference email from Miyahuna to MCA-J on 12/7, saying that it is not possible for Miyahuna to measure customer meters (by area) or wastewater subscribers in non MCC DMAs. Miyahuna claims they have never collected this data and cannot publish any historical figures. title.narrative: Continuity of service

description.narrative: Level Outcome of '- The measurement of Non-Revenue Water in Zarqa is highly variable and prone to measurement error. NRW is composed of two key data sources: the amount of water entering the network and the amount of water leaving the network. In Q3 of 2014, Miyahuna-Zarqa installed inflow meters on their network and began measuring the amount of water supplied to the network in Zarqa. All the measured amounts of water supplied to Zarqa prior to the installation of those meters were estimates. These meters represent significant improvements in the quality of measurement of the inflow of water to Zarqa. - Similar strides have not yet been made in measuring the amount of water leaving the network in Zarqa. Miyahuna-Zarqa measures an estimate of 80 percent of the customer meters in their network every quarter, which does not align with the monthly inflow measures. As a result, they use a combination of data, forecasting, and estimation to calculate how much water has left the network. In addition, there are often an unknown number of outflow points in any part of the network, making it extremely challenging to hydrologically isolate portions of the network to accurately capture NRW. This introduces significant measurement error and helps explain the sizeable variance in the NRW figure from quarter to quarter. - Due to these well-known challenges in data quality, a baseline that is simply a measurement of NRW in one quarter will likely be inaccurate and could vary by as much as ten points the next quarter. To account for the variation and insure that the assessment of Compact results is not disproportionately impacted by measurement error, the MCC and MCA-J team believe that the best approach is to take an average of the quarters after the new inflow meters came online and the first portion of the MCC investment as operationalized. - Separate measurements are underway to independently and accurately report NRW within MCC DMAs in order to identify the magnitude of the MCC investment. Similarly, steps are being taken to identify an area outside of MCC DMAs that accurately portrays the NRW figure for the entire governorate outside of MCC DMAs. The aim is that these more refined measures provide nuance to an otherwise qualitatively poor figure. -Reference to an Email between MCC and the M&E director, it was agreed on shifting all actuals to the left by one quarter in Q18 to reflect the data of these quarters. - This figure is the official NRW calculation reported by Miyahuna in Jordan.

title.narrative: Continuity of supply (Non MCC DMAs)

description.narrative: Level Outcome of MCC conducted an exercise to isolate the continuity of supply in MCC DMAs and non MCC DMAs. This was done to ensure proper data quality in order to quantify the benefit brought by MCC's investment. Miyahuna's supply scheme is demand based. The operator monitors the supplied volume at the distribution tank. When customers demand is satisfied, the amount supplied to the network decrease. This creates a build up in water volumes in the distribution tank. The operator then stops the supply and shift it to a neighboring DMA. The supply time in non MCC DMAs was measured to be higher due to the fact that there are higher leakages in this network and a longer supply time is needed to reach the same amount of water quantity.

description.narrative: Cumulative Output of The work in WSH ISW started in June of 2015 and has been finished contractually in end of May 2016. This is the last available data reported through Q20. Quarterly data corresponds to the Monthly Progress Reports received during that corresponding quarter. While CoWater notes a total of 63,993 people who attended the awareness sessions in their final MPR 25 report, the ITT is justified in cumulatively measuring 64,002. This is due to the fact that CoWater admits to verifying and continuing to work on data inconsistencies between monthly reports (see around pg 10 of each report where CoWater states this). Discussions between MCC and CoWater will continue as these inconsistencies are worked through. It should also be noted that while these data inconsistencies have resulted in challenges segregating the data between men and women, the sessions were attended by mostly females.
